passage:
Subject: sorry, and a real question
Maria,
When Professor Rao tore into our joint poster on Tuesday, I'd shrugged it off by dinner. That's how I am: criticism rolls off, I fix the thing, I sleep fine. So on Wednesday I sent you a cheerful list of edits and a silly cartoon, and I didn't notice you'd gone quiet until Ana told me you skipped the lab meeting. I think I assumed you'd bounced back like I did. That wasn't fair. So, properly this time: how are you doing with it? Not the poster, you. If you want to talk, or just sit in the canteen without talking, I'm free after four.
Chaitanya

qa.q: By when had Chaitanya shrugged off Professor Rao's criticism?
qa.a: By dinner.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya think Maria was feeling after Tuesday?
qa.a: Chaitanya assumed Maria had bounced back and felt as calm as Chaitanya did, so Chaitanya didn't notice Maria had gone quiet.

qa.q: What choice does Chaitanya make in the email?
qa.a: Chaitanya apologises for assuming and asks directly how Maria is, offering to talk or just sit together after four.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt receiving the cheerful list of edits on Wednesday?
qa.a: Maria may have felt more alone, as if the hurt didn't count while everyone else moved on.

grounding: A calm young adult who recovers fast from criticism realises a friend was struggling and asks instead of assuming.

passage: Vasudha asked me last night, "Karthik, how are you never rattled?" Honestly? When I didn't get the internship in June, I was disappointed for one evening, then I made a new list and applied to six more. When the coach yells at practice, I keep the useful bit and forget the volume. That's how I'm built. But I got it wrong with Vasudha herself. Her cousin was in hospital last month, and I kept saying, "It'll be fine, don't overthink." I thought I was helping. She finally told me it made her feel silly for being scared. So now I try something new. I ask, "Do you want solutions or company?" Mostly she says company.

qa.q: How long was Karthik disappointed after missing the internship?
qa.a: For one evening.

qa.q: What did Karthik think those words would do when Karthik said "It'll be fine, don't overthink"?
qa.a: Karthik thought they were helping, not realising it made Vasudha feel silly for being scared.

qa.q: What new question does Karthik now ask, and why is it a better choice?
qa.a: "Do you want solutions or company?" It lets Vasudha say what she needs instead of Karthik assuming.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when told not to overthink while her cousin was in hospital?
qa.a: She felt silly for being scared, as if her worry was not allowed.

grounding: A young adult who bounces back easily learns that a friend's worry was bigger than assumed and starts asking what she needs.

passage: The agriculture diploma results came out on the same afternoon in Hoshangabad. Himani had missed the merit list by a few ranks. She read it twice, sighed, and by evening had pinned next year's form to the wall. 'One exam,' she said. 'Not the end of the world.' Her cousin Vikas had missed it too. Over tea she told him the same thing, cheerfully. 'Chill, na. Next year.' He nodded. For three days after that he didn't come to the dairy where they both helped. On the fourth, Himani found him by the canal, throwing stones. She almost said 'chill' again. Instead she sat down. 'I think I assumed it hit you the way it hit me. How bad is it, really?' Vikas threw another stone. 'Bad,' he said. 'Papa had already told everyone I'd get in.' She stayed till dark, mostly listening.

qa.q: What had Himani pinned to the wall by evening?
qa.a: Next year's form.

qa.q: How did Himani feel on missing the merit list?
qa.a: She was briefly disappointed but calm and steady, sighing and planning for next year within hours.

qa.q: What did Himani do differently by the canal, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked how bad it really was instead of saying 'chill', which let Vikas admit the pressure he was under.

qa.q: What might Himani's cheerful 'Chill, na' have felt like to Vikas?
qa.a: It probably left Vikas feeling alone and brushed off, since he was struggling far more and dreading what his father had told everyone.

grounding: Shows a young adult who recovers quickly from a setback, assumes her cousin feels the same, and learns to ask rather than assume.

passage: At the Tuesday design critique in Melbourne, the lecturer tore into Mina's poster: 'Cluttered, no hierarchy, start again.' Mina wrote it down, nodded, and was sketching a new version on the tram home, humming. That evening she knocked on her flatmate Mei's door. Mei had got almost the same comments. 'Dumplings? It's only one crit.' 'Not hungry,' Mei said through the door. Mina shrugged; people bounced back, she figured. But by Thursday Mei still hadn't touched her poster, and her light was on at three in the morning. Mina made two cups of tea and knocked again. 'I think I've been assuming you're like me about criticism. Are you?' A long pause. The door opened. 'No,' Mei said, eyes red. 'I've been thinking about leaving the course.' Mina sat down on the floor. 'Tell me.'

qa.q: What did the lecturer say about Mina's poster?
qa.a: 'Cluttered, no hierarchy, start again.'

qa.q: How did Mina feel after the harsh critique?
qa.a: Mina felt calm and unbothered, humming and sketching a new version on the tram home.

qa.q: What could Mina suggest after hearing Mei out?
qa.a: After listening, Mina could offer to go with Mei to a tutor or student adviser before any decision about leaving.

qa.q: What were the days after the critique like for Mei?
qa.a: Mei was hurt and struggling, not eating, awake at three, even thinking of leaving the course.

grounding: Shows a young adult who shrugs off criticism, assumes her flatmate does too, and then asks instead of assuming.

passage: By the end of his first month at the insurance helpline, Tushar had a reputation: nothing rattled him. When a caller shouted at him for ten minutes, he took notes, said, 'I understand, sir,' and afterwards stretched and fetched a coffee. 'Part of the job,' he said. At the next desk, Preeti's call ended with the customer swearing at her. She took off her headset and walked out. Tushar assumed she'd be back in five minutes, like him. She wasn't. Twenty minutes later he found her on the stairwell, knees pulled up. He was about to say, 'Don't take it personally.' He stopped. 'That sounded rough. What was it like for you?' Preeti wiped her face. 'He said things about my voice. I keep hearing them.' Tushar sat a step below her. 'Want me to tell the team lead? You shouldn't have to take the next call yet.'

qa.q: What did Tushar say when a caller shouted at him?
qa.a: 'I understand, sir.'

qa.q: How did Tushar feel after being shouted at for ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt calm and unshaken, taking notes and stretching afterwards.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's offer to tell the team lead a good step?
qa.a: It turned concern into practical support, getting Preeti a break and involving the person in charge of the calls.

qa.q: What was that call like for Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti felt hurt and shaken by the caller's comments about her voice, and couldn't stop hearing them.

grounding: Shows a calm young adult who rarely spirals over criticism, nearly underestimates a colleague's distress, and asks instead of assuming.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I keep thinking about Tuesday, when Dr Rao handed back our project covered in red ink. I shrugged, said "Fine, we fix it," and went off to buy samosas. You went very quiet. Later I told you, "It's just one grade, don't stress," and you left early.
Honestly, criticism mostly slides off me. I sleep on it and wake up ready to redo things. I think I assumed you worked the same way, and I talked right over whatever you were feeling.
So I'd like to ask instead of guess. How are you doing with it? Would it help to split the fixes differently, or to just talk first? I'm free Thursday after four, and this time I'll bring the samosas to you.
Parveen

qa.q: What did Parveen say to Elizabeth later that day?
qa.a: Parveen said, "It's just one grade, don't stress."

qa.q: How does Parveen feel now about Tuesday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Parveen feels sorry and a bit uneasy, admitting to having assumed Elizabeth worked the same way and to having talked over Elizabeth's feelings.

qa.q: What makes this email a good next step?
qa.a: It asks Elizabeth how things are going instead of guessing, offers choices about the fixes, and suggests a set time to talk.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt on hearing "don't stress"?
qa.a: Elizabeth may have felt brushed aside and more alone with the worry, which fits going quiet and leaving early.

grounding: Shows a calm young adult who bounces back from criticism realising a teammate took it harder and choosing to ask rather than assume.
